items.title: A struct literal evaluates its field initializers in DECLARATION order on the JS backend and in WRITTEN order natively — `Point { y = say("y", 2), x = say("x", 1) }` prints x, y on JS and y, x on native
items.body: B452's `walk_siblings_in_order` walks the fields as written and spills an earlier sibling only when a later one lowers to statements; the JS array is then laid out in declaration order, so two plain calls run in layout order. vilan-rust emits a Rust struct literal, which evaluates as written. The two backends disagree on a side-effecting initializer, and the native differential has no probe for it. Fix as B569 S2 did for a tuple literal matched by name (`Program::tuple_literal_layouts`): when the written order is not the layout, bind every unsettled initializer to a `const` in written order, then lay out. Repro: finds/struct_literal_evaluates_in_declaration_order.vl. Sizing S; transformer.

items.title: A tuple-typed `[rpc]` parameter or `[derive(Wire)]` field is refused quoting its type as `_` — "parameter `message` of `[rpc]` method `echo` is `_`, which is not Wire"
items.body: `render_type` (analyzer.rs) renders a name, a generic application and a `::` path as written and falls back to `_` for every other form; a tuple (labelled or not), an array and a closure type are the common cases. The refusal is right (tuples have no Wire impl; a user `impl (i32, i32) with Wire` is not consulted by these syntactic checks either), the quote is not. `render_type` also feeds the derive generators' emitted source, so the fix is a separate quoting path for the messages, not a wider `render_type` (lang-a-49 tried the wider one: the Wire derive then emitted `(x: i32, y: i32)` where its generated code needs an expression path, and failed later and worse). Repro: finds/tuple_quoted_as_underscore.vl. Sizing XS.

items.title: A spread of a tuple LITERAL into a spread parameter (`draw(..(3, 4))`) is refused natively — "does not emit a spread element whose tuple type did not resolve yet" — while JS runs it
items.body: `draw(..p)` over a binding builds natively; spreading the literal itself does not, labelled or not (B569 S4 met it with `draw(..(x = 3, y = 4))`). The spread operand's own tuple type is not recorded for a literal operand (`tuple_element_types` covers elements, not a spread operand), which `spread_tuple` reads. Repro: finds/native_spread_of_a_tuple_literal.vl. Sizing S; vilan-rust (or the analyzer's record for a spread operand).
